newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan Kubo says will work for stronger recovery.
newsitem.headline: Japan Kubo says will work for stronger recovery.

text.p: The Japanese government will continue to work towards ensuring a stronger and sustainable economic recovery, Finance Minister Wataru Kubo said on Friday.

"We want to continue to work towards strengthening the economic recovery and ensuring its sustainability by steadily implementing the 1996/97 budget and quickly coping with the problem loans of financial instituions," Kubo told a meeting of life insurers.

The Japanese economy is continuing to recover on the back of increasingly firm private-sector demand, but the pace of the recovery remains gradual due to lingering worries over employment conditions, Kubo said.
He also stressed the need for Japan to tackle fiscal reforms to reduce its escalating deficit, which would help maintain the vitality and stable growth of the economy.
The Japanese cabinet decided on June 25 to implement a planned increase in the consumption tax to five percent from the current three percent from April 1997, he said.
"We will work to smoothly implement this," Kubo said.
The government's decision has been met with opposition even within the main ruling coalition party ahead of general elections rumoured to be called as early as next month.
He also urged financial institutions to finish dealing with problem loans as soon as possible and work diligently towards better risk management and company restructuring.

In response to criticism that the government has not been able to accurately gauge the state of these institutions due to inadequate supervision and inspection, Kubo said, "There is a need for a drastic turnaround in the government's administration of the financial sector."
He added that the ministry would aim for the supervision of the financial industry based on market rules and a policy of asking companies to take responsibility for their own actions.

On the insurance issue, Japan and the United States remain far apart over their interpretation of the bilateral insurance pact, but Kubo said Japan would put its utmost effort into settling the issue as soon as possible.
A round of marathon negotiations took place in Vancouver, British Columbia, in late July to resolve the dispute but no agreement was reached.

A senior MOF official said on Thursday that the insurance talks will likely be resumed later this month, but added it remains unclear if the two nations will be able to start working-level negotiations next week.
